1.question: A message says you have won ₹50,000 in a mobile-recharge lottery, and asks for a ₹999 "processing fee" to release it. What is the biggest red flag?
options: The fee is a round number
Genuine prizes are never released by first collecting a fee from the winner
The message uses the word 'lucky draw'
The amount is too large to be real
1.explanation: Legitimate lotteries or rewards deduct tax/fees from the winnings itself — they never ask winners to pay money upfront to 'unlock' a prize.

1.question: You get a message that looks exactly like it is from your manager ("Priya"), asking you to urgently buy ₹10000 in gift cards and send the codes because they are "in a meeting and can't call." What should you do?
options: Comply quickly since it sounds urgent
Verify through a separate channel (a phone call) before taking any action
Reply asking for more details over the same chat
Ignore it completely without checking
1.explanation: Impersonation scams rely on urgency and an inability to verify in the moment. A quick call to the real person on a known number instantly exposes the scam.

1.question: You search online for a food delivery app customer care about a failed refund, wait 2 minutes, and call a number from the results. The agent asks you to install a remote-access app "to fix the issue faster." What is the danger here?
options: Remote apps use too much data
It will slow down your phone
Remote-access tools give the caller full control of your device, including banking apps
Support calls are always free anyway
1.explanation: Fake customer-care numbers are frequently seeded on the open web. Once a scammer has remote access, they can open your banking apps directly — never install remote-access software at the request of an unsolicited 'support' call.

1.question: An SMS says: "HDFC Bank: Your account will be suspended in 45 minutes. Verify now: bit.ly/verify-192". What is the strongest warning sign?
options: The message is written in formal English
The email/SMS uses your first name
The message arrived during business hours
Urgency + an unofficial shortened link asking you to 'verify'
1.explanation: Legitimate banks never create artificial time pressure and never send verification links to look-alike domains. Always type the bank's known URL directly instead of clicking a link in an unsolicited message.

1.question: Someone calling from a delivery partner asks you to read out the OTP you just received to "cancel a fraudulent transaction" of ₹12504. What should you do?
options: It is safe since they already know your card details
Refuse and hang up — never share an OTP with anyone who calls you
It is needed to confirm your identity to the bank
Reading it out loud does not share it electronically
1.explanation: An OTP is a one-time authorization code. No legitimate process ever requires you to read it to someone else — doing so approves whatever transaction the scammer initiated.
